meta.title: Data modes and SSR
meta.description: Holding the items yourself, fetching them per rendered range, and rendering the schedule on a server without a hydration warning.

basics.intro: The component never fetches. You hold items, and it renders what you hold. That leaves two ways to work: give it everything you have, or give it what the rendered range needs and refill as the range moves.
basics.range: onVisibleRangeChange fires on mount and whenever the rendered range changes — a new date, a different shift pattern, more shifts before or after. It is the signal to fetch. While the answer is on its way, keep loading on: the items already on screen stay there, dimmed, instead of blanking.

server.intro: The component renders on a server without touching the DOM, and hydrates without a warning in React 18 and 19. The first frame is deliberately the plain one:
points: Compact mode is off unless you pass the boolean yourself — width cannot be measured on a server.
Nothing is pinned, because pinning is a scroll position.
The clock starts from now, or from defaultDate when you give neither. Passing now is what makes the two renders agree exactly.
The server-rendered markup is the same structure the client hydrates: a reader without JavaScript gets the schedule, its headings and its item names.
Nothing about the states is announced twice across hydration: the live regions start empty and only speak on a change.
A refresh that keeps the old items visible keeps the reading position too, which matters most for someone navigating by keyboard.
onVisibleRangeChange for fetching, loading and error for what the reader sees meanwhile — see States.
now makes the render deterministic, which is also what the visual tests of this package rely on.
<link to="/integrations/nextjs/">Next.js</link> and <link to="/integrations/ssr/">Server rendering</link> have the framework-specific parts.
There is no built-in cache, no request deduplication and no retry: that is your data layer’s job.
The overflow dialog is not paged from a server; it shows the items of the group it already has.
A range change is reported after it happened, so a fetch always begins with the new range already rendered — empty, loading, or with the previous items.
